justification: Adds a refusal inside the two code paths that write live regulatory provisions to the single production database. A wrong guard either lets a worse extraction replace good rules again, or blocks legitimate council amendments from ever going live.

falsifiable_check.fails_when: the commit job commits a chapter whose live section codes fall from 38 to 8 without --allow-section-loss naming that chapter, or the monitor image stops copying the guard module both workers import
falsifiable_check.observed_red: With the enforce_section_loss call deleted from dcp_commit_approved.py and the guard COPY deleted from Dockerfile.monitors: assert conn.commits == 0 -> E assert 1 == 0 ('a swap losing 30 of 38 sections was committed'); assert dca.main() == 1 -> E assert (2 == 1); Missing COPY in Dockerfile.monitors: scripts/dcp_commit_approved.py imports scripts.dcp_supersede_guard; 3 failed, 6 passed. Restored: 9 passed. Row rule forced off (if False): test_keeping_every_section_but_few_rules_is_refused and test_the_row_bar_is_more_than_three_quarters_and_is_bounded_both_ways FAILED, 2 failed 10 passed; restored, 12 passed.

pre_impl.existing_data: Measured 2026-09-13 on production: marrickville part4-s1-low-density live version had 26 rules and 8 section codes while the switched-off earlier version had 215 rules and 38 codes; mixed use 225 to 19; stormwater 16 codes to 1.
pre_impl.assumption_mismatch: The commit path assumed an approved version is at least as good as the live one. Approval is per row, so nobody reviewing rows sees that whole sections vanished; AI extraction is non-deterministic between runs.
pre_impl.new_vs_existing: dcp_extract_changed already had a row-count gate (is_count_drop) but only on its own path and only on row counts; dcp_commit_approved had no comparison at all. This adds one section-code check shared by both.
pre_impl.external_source_error: The guard reads nothing external. If the database query fails, the exception rolls the transaction back and the chapter is not committed, which fails closed rather than writing unmeasured.
pre_impl.frontend_type: No frontend change. The page reads regulatory_provisions through app/api/provisions/for-property, which this change does not touch; it only affects which version becomes current.
pre_impl.user_failure_mode: Without the guard a property report silently loses setbacks, heights and floor space rules for a whole chapter. With a mistuned guard a real council amendment never goes live and the daily job fails loudly instead.

functions.name: snapshot
functions.input: An open cursor inside the caller's transaction, a council slug and a chapter key.
functions.output: A Snapshot holding the set of leading section codes of the chapter's current rows and the current row count.
functions.if_none: A chapter with no current rows returns an empty code set and zero rows; NULL section headers count as rows with no code.

functions.name: judge
functions.input: Two Snapshots of the same chapter: before the write and after it, within one transaction.
functions.output: A Verdict: refused when more than half the section codes are gone, or when sections survive but more than three-quarters of the rules are gone; with the measure, counts, lost codes and new codes.
functions.if_none: An empty before snapshot is not judged and is allowed, so a first extraction of a new chapter always passes.

functions.name: enforce
functions.input: Cursor, council, chapter key, the before Snapshot, and the set of council/chapter names a person allowed.
functions.output: The Verdict when allowed; raises SectionLossRefused naming the numbers and the exact override flag when refused.
functions.if_none: An empty allowed set means nothing is overridden, which is what every scheduled run passes, so scheduled runs fail closed.

values.if_missing: NULL header counts as a row with no section code; if too few codes exist the chapter is judged by row count instead.

queries.purpose: Read the live section headers of one chapter before and after a commit, inside the same transaction
queries.where_clause: source_council = %s AND source_chapter_key = %s AND is_current = TRUE

break_it.scenario: A council genuinely renumbers a chapter, so every old section code disappears and new ones replace them one for one.
break_it.what_happens: The guard refuses a legitimate amendment and the daily commit job fails until someone acts.
break_it.how: Deliberate: every served citation changes, which a person should see. The refusal prints how many new codes arrived so a renumbering is recognisable, and --allow-section-loss council/chapter lets exactly that chapter through.

break_it.scenario: Headers in the old version are bare control markers such as C7, which leading_code also reads as codes, inflating the before count.
break_it.what_happens: More codes look lost than real sections, so a borderline swap is refused that arguably should pass.
break_it.how: This errs toward refusing, never toward letting a loss through, and the override exists for the checked case. Found by sampling marrickville tree-management, whose 25 codes were control markers.
break_it.repro: python -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'scripts'); from dcp_chapter_measure import leading_code; print(leading_code('C7 C7'))"

break_it.scenario: A refusal happens inside the unattended Railway cron and nobody reads the log.
break_it.what_happens: The better rules stay live, but a pending approval sits refused forever with no one aware.
break_it.how: A refusal is counted as a failed chapter, so dcp_commit_approved exits 1, which run_monitors treats as a failure and alerts on. The test asserts the exit code, not just the message.

break_it.scenario: The direct-commit branch of dcp_extract_changed.extract_chapter swaps a chapter without going through the review queue.
break_it.what_happens: If its wiring were wrong the same loss could land by the on-demand path even though the commit job is protected.
break_it.how: Wired the same way (snapshot before the first write, enforce before conn.commit) and the module-level import is pinned by the packaging test, but no behavioural test drives extract_chapter, which needs a PDF, R2 and preflight. Production cron runs extraction with --review, which never commits.

break_it.scenario: A chapter whose rows carry no section codes at all, like ashfield's 747 uncoded rows, is replaced by a much smaller version.
break_it.what_happens: A code-only rule would see nothing to lose and wave the collapse through.
break_it.how: Below five codes the guard judges by row count: more than 20 rows before and more than half gone is refused.

break_it.scenario: The guard is added in code but the Railway monitor image is not rebuilt with the new module.
break_it.what_happens: Both DCP workers crash at import with ModuleNotFoundError on their next scheduled run.
break_it.how: Dockerfile.monitors copies dcp_supersede_guard.py and dcp_chapter_measure.py, and test_every_sibling_import_is_copied_into_the_image went red when the COPY was removed.

break_it.scenario: A broken run emits exactly one rule per section, so every section code survives while most of the rules are deleted.
break_it.what_happens: A guard that only compares section codes allows it, and the chapter silently loses 177 of its 215 rules.
break_it.how: Cross-review round 1 (HIGH, real). With sections measurable the guard also refuses when more than three-quarters of the rules are gone. The bar is 75 percent rather than 50 so a consolidation like Waverley 607 to 264 rules, one rule per clause instead of objectives and controls apart, still passes. Forcing the row rule off turned two tests red.
break_it.repro: python -m pytest tests/test_dcp_supersede_guard.py -k "few_rules or row_bar or consolidation" -q

post_merge.db_reset: No. No schema change and no data change; the guard only reads.
post_merge.manual_verify: Yes: the monitor image rebuilds on merge. Read the next dcp-commit deploy log on Railway and confirm it starts without ImportError.
